decision: Target draft-pantos-hls-rfc8216bis (HTTP Live Streaming 2nd Edition), pinned to revision -22, over RFC 8216. The revision's text is vendored into the repo and its section layout sets the module tree.
rationale: RFC 8216 lacks Low-Latency HLS, EXT-X-DEFINE, content steering, and interstitial DATERANGE attributes that current manifests use. The code can mirror only one document's numbering, and pinning one revision keeps section numbers stable until a deliberate upgrade.
trigger: The user asked for a copy of the HLS RFC in the repo, with code structured to match its layout. That raised the question of which spec version to vendor.

decision: Decisions are tracked in work/decisions/decisions.jsonl, one JSON object per line, recording the decision, who made it, and what brought it up. A work/backlog directory sits beside it.
rationale: The user asked for a durable in-repo record of every decision and its provenance.
trigger: The user's reply approving decision 1.

decision: The backlog is work/backlog/backlog.jsonl, one item per line, using the same JSONL shape as the decision log.
rationale: The user specified a format for decisions but not for the backlog. Using the same format for both means one set of tools reads them.
trigger: Creating the work/backlog directory from decision 2. Trivial and reversible, so decided without asking.

decision: Revision -22 is confirmed as the latest rfc8216bis revision (published 2026-05-01). Its stated expiry of 2026-11-02 has passed, while Datatracker still labels it Active. The pin stays on -22.
rationale: An expired draft is still the most recent text of the spec, and a newer revision would replace it through decision 1's diff-and-update path.
trigger: Decision 1 committed to verifying the revision on Datatracker before vendoring.

decision: Mode is selected by overloading parse on its input type: a string parses statically and synchronously, and an AsyncIterable<string> parses in streaming mode, asynchronously. The reviver stays the second argument in both, as in JSON.parse(text, reviver). There is no mode flag.
rationale: The input type already determines the mode, so a flag repeats it and permits contradictory calls. Overloads give each call shape its own return type and keep the JSON.parse call shape. Static is the default because the string call shape needs no flag.
trigger: The requirement for two modes, streaming over an AsyncIterable and static over a string with static as the default, under an interface matching the JSON builtin.

decision: Streaming parse returns an AsyncIterable of complete units in document order: each media segment once its URI line arrives, each variant stream at its URI, and playlist-level tags as they appear. Checks that span the whole playlist run at the end, and a failure rejects the iterator's final step. The reviver runs on each yielded unit. Units form a union keyed by kind.
rationale: A long VOD playlist is where streaming pays off. Returning Promise<Playlist> makes the caller wait for the last byte and hold every segment. The spec's ordering rules (EXT-X-DEFINE before use, segment tags before the URI) make each unit final when it is yielded. A Playlist can be recovered by collecting the iterable.
trigger: Decision 5 made streaming mode asynchronous over an AsyncIterable, which left the shape of its output open.

decision: HLS.safeParse is the core API and returns an outcome union keyed by kind (parsed with a playlist, or malformed with issues). HLS.parse wraps it and throws a SyntaxError whose cause is the issues, matching JSON.parse. In streaming mode, safeParse yields a final malformed unit where parse rejects. The throw in parse is the library's only throw site and is a declared exception to the style guide's no-throw-for-known-outcomes rule. It carries a why-comment, and style/no-throw's warning on that line is accepted in review.
rationale: The JSON builtin throws, while the style guide makes a malformed playlist a returned outcome. The zod-style pair keeps parse drop-in compatible with JSON.parse and gives callers who branch on outcomes a non-throwing path.
trigger: Matching JSON.parse's SyntaxError conflicts with the style guide's rule that known outcomes are return values.

decision: Malformed means exactly the spec's 'clients MUST fail to parse' rules (12 sites in -22), and forward-compatible ignoring follows section 6.3.1 exactly. Other MUSTs a playlist breaks are reported as non-fatal violations on the parsed outcome of safeParse, and parse drops them. Each rule carries its spec citation and its default severity, and severity is resolved through one policy lookup from rule to severity. A future strictness option (lenient, or a per-rule override) would then be a different policy table, with no change to the checks. That option is not built now.
rationale: The spec already states which violations are fatal. Violations make the library usable as a validator without rejecting playlists that players accept. Strictness is a known axis of evolution, so the seam is reserved now while the option itself waits.
trigger: Decision 7 created a malformed outcome, which left open which spec violations produce it. The user chose the spec's own line and required that a strictness option remain possible later.

decision: Both JSONL files are append-only. A line is never edited or removed. A correction or status change is a new line that refers back to the earlier one: an amends field in the decision log, and a repeated id in the backlog, where the latest line for an id gives its current state.
rationale: The log is a history of how each decision was reached, and editing a line in place destroys that history.
trigger: Claude rewrote backlog item 1's line in place to mark it done. That line was restored to its original text and the status change was appended as a new line.

decision: Decision 6's example of an end-of-playlist check is replaced. Segment durations exceeding the target duration (section 4.4.3.1) is a requirement on servers, so under decision 8 it is a non-fatal violation and does not reject the iterator. An example of a check that does reject is a playlist containing both Media Segment tags and Multivariant Playlist tags (section 4.4.4).
rationale: The vendored spec separates client fail-to-parse rules from server requirements, and decision 6 cited a rule from the wrong category.
trigger: Reading the vendored -22 text while preparing the strictness question.

decision: Output keys for things the spec defines use the spec's names verbatim (variant["AVERAGE-BANDWIDTH"], playlist["EXT-X-TARGETDURATION"]). Structure the library adds that the spec does not name (segments, variants, kind) uses camelCase TypeScript naming.
rationale: The user asked for names matching the objects represented. Verbatim keys can be searched in the vendored spec and keep one name per meaning across spec and code. The library's own containers are extensions the spec has no name for. Bracket access is the cost, and TypeScript autocompletes and checks it.
trigger: The requirement that output objects match the values, properties, and names of the objects they represent.

decision: Each spec value type (section 4.2) maps to exactly one TypeScript type with no per-attribute exceptions. decimal-integer becomes bigint. decimal-floating-point and signed-decimal-floating-point become number. quoted-string becomes string with the quotes removed. enumerated-string becomes a literal union derived from an as-const object. enumerated-string-list becomes a readonly array of that union, with unrecognized members dropped. hexadecimal-sequence stays a string in its spec text. decimal-resolution becomes { width: bigint; height: bigint }.
rationale: The spec defines decimal-integer as 64-bit, and number silently loses precision above 2^53. A rounded media sequence identifies the wrong segment. JSON.stringify throwing on bigint is the accepted cost. Byte arrays cannot be frozen, so hexadecimal stays a string to keep the output truly readonly. One type per spec type keeps the mapping predictable.
trigger: Decision 11 fixed the output keys, which left the value types under them open.

decision: Decision 8's count of 12 parse-failure sites is wrong. -22 has 13 MUST-level parse-failure rules: 12 'MUST fail to parse', counting one split across a line break, plus 'MUST trigger a parsing error' for undefined variable references in section 6.3.1. It also has 3 SHOULD-level ones: 'SHOULD fail to parse' for a BOM or invalid UTF-8, and 'SHOULD refuse to parse' for a missing EXTM3U identification and for duplicate AttributeNames. The rule inventory is built by reading each section, not by searching for phrases, because a phrase split by a page footer escapes search. How the SHOULD-level rules are classified is open.
rationale: The earlier count came from a single-line search that matched only one phrasing.
trigger: Reading section 6.3.1 while preparing the variable-substitution question.

decision: The 3 SHOULD-level parse refusals (BOM or invalid UTF-8, missing EXTM3U identification, duplicate AttributeName) default to malformed in the decision 8 policy table. A future lenient policy may downgrade them.
rationale: None of the three yields a sound result. A duplicate attribute forces an arbitrary winner, text without EXTM3U may not be a playlist at all, and a BOM or invalid UTF-8 means the bytes are corrupt or mis-encoded.
trigger: Decision 13 found SHOULD-level parse refusals that decision 8 did not classify.

decision: Substitution context is an optional { uri?: URL; multivariant?: MultivariantPlaylist } object. parse and safeParse are overloaded so it is passed either third, after a reviver, as in parse(text, reviver, context), or second, with no reviver, as in parse(text, context). A function in second position is the reviver and an object is the context. These shapes combine with decision 5's string and AsyncIterable overloads. NAME variables are always substituted. IMPORT without multivariant, and QUERYPARAM without a uri or with no matching parameter, produce malformed as the spec requires. Keeping JSON.parse's positional (text, reviver) is a declared exception to the style guide's rule that three or more parameters go through an options object.
rationale: The first two positions are fixed by JSON.parse, and the context extends beyond them. The overload means a caller with only context never writes a placeholder reviver. Taking a parsed MultivariantPlaylist lets the library read its definitions, so callers cannot pass a mismatched variable set.
trigger: The spec requires variable substitution, and IMPORT and QUERYPARAM need context a string does not carry. The user chose an optional context argument and required an overload that drops the reviver.

decision: A hand-written line scanner (a loop, with one small regex per token) produces raw tags: a name and attributes as unparsed strings. Each tag's zod schema converts and validates the raw form in one .safeParse call. The schema lives in its spec section's module and is that section's attribute table in code. Because these schemas transform, they are called with .safeParse directly, the style guide's stated exception to assertSchema, and zod issue paths become malformed issues.
rationale: Each spec rule lives in one place. The scanner stays small, linear, and bounded per line. Validating only the finished output would write every rule twice, and zod over the whole text would put the grammar into one large regex.
trigger: The requirements for a fast parser and for zod used internally pull against each other.

decision: The library has two entry points. The default entry uses the runtime zod parser with no compilation. A separate precompiled entry applies z.compile explicitly to each tag schema. Neither entry imports zod/compile or sets jitless, so neither changes the host app's global zod config. A test runs z.compile(schema, { strict: true }) over every schema so a schema that silently stops compiling fails CI. Schemas convert with transform or pipe, never z.coerce (which the compiler refuses), and apply .readonly() at every level so the output is frozen at runtime.
rationale: z.compile generates code with new Function, which CSP and Cloudflare Workers block. The default entry works everywhere, and environments that allow eval opt into the faster path. zod/compile installs a hook on the global config, which a library must not do to its host.
trigger: Claude's research into zod 4.5+ compilation found that it depends on new Function. The user required separate compiled and uncompiled entry points, with uncompiled as the default.

decision: The core is a factory, createHLS(schemas), taking the table of tag schemas as an argument. Each tag schema stays in its spec section's module (decision 16), and the table is assembled from those modules. The default entry calls the factory with the schemas as they are. The precompiled entry maps z.compile over the table once at startup and passes the result, using a mapped type that keeps each tag's schema type. Both entries export identical types and are independent instances.
rationale: z.compile returns a clone and leaves the original untouched, so compiled schemas only take effect if the parsing code reads them from the table it was given. A factory makes the compiled table belong to its entry alone, independent of import order and without global state.
trigger: Decision 17's two entry points needed a way for the precompiled entry to swap in compiled schemas. The user weighed importing zod/compile and a zod registry, then chose the factory.

decision: The library uses no zod registry, global or private, and never calls .describe() or .meta(). A rule's spec citation is plain data next to its schema in its section module.
rationale: zod's global registry is process-wide. Entries with an id are held strongly and overwritten silently on collision, and the host's z.toJSONSchema(z.globalRegistry) emits them. Namespacing ids prevents collisions with the host but not that output leak, and not collisions between two installed versions of the library. A zod registry also has no public iteration and erases each tag's type, so the factory table (decision 18) does the job without one.
trigger: Decision 8 requires each rule to carry its citation, and .meta() is the obvious way to attach one. The user asked about namespacing registry entries and about using a registry to drive compilation.

decision: The reviver follows JSON.parse exactly. It is called as reviver.call(holder, key, value) on every property, children before parents, ending with key "" on the root, and returning undefined removes the property. The root is the playlist in static mode and each unit in streaming mode. Passing a reviver makes the result type unknown. The reviver runs before freezing.
rationale: JSON.parse parity is the point of the API, so revivers written for the builtin work unchanged. TypeScript cannot follow arbitrary replacement through the tree, so unknown is the honest type. The per-property walk costs nothing when no reviver is passed.
trigger: Decisions 5 and 6 kept the reviver argument without saying what it is called with.

decision: The streaming parse is overloaded on AsyncIterable<string> and AsyncIterable<Uint8Array>, chosen by chunk type. Byte chunks are decoded with new TextDecoder("utf-8", { fatal: true, ignoreBOM: true }), which reports invalid UTF-8 and keeps a BOM so it can be reported. String chunks are checked for a leading U+FEFF and for lone surrogates. Static mode stays string-only, like JSON.parse.
rationale: fetch bodies and file streams produce bytes, and decision 14's invalid-UTF-8 rule can only be enforced on bytes. A string has already been decoded, possibly lossily.
trigger: Decision 14 made invalid UTF-8 malformed, while decision 5 assumed string chunks, on which that rule cannot be checked.

decision: The package ships ESM only, compiled to ES2024, with engines.node >=22.12 and current browsers. No module may use top-level await, and a test asserts it.
rationale: require(esm) is on by default from Node 22.12 and stable on every supported LTS line (Node 20 reached end of life on 2026-04-30), so CommonJS consumers can still load the package. A dual build would serve only end-of-life Node versions. ES2024 provides String.prototype.isWellFormed for decision 21. Top-level await makes require() throw ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE.
trigger: Decision 21's lone-surrogate check depends on an ES2024 method, which raised the question of runtime targets and module format.

decision: A tag with no value is true when present, with its key absent otherwise. A single-value tag is its value. A compound-value tag is an object keyed by the spec's prose nouns. An attribute-list tag is an object keyed by attribute name. A playlist is MediaPlaylist | MultivariantPlaylist, discriminated by kind with values media and multivariant. A tag that can appear only once is a property, and a tag that can repeat is a readonly array under its tag name. Media segments go in segments, each with its URI and preceding segment tags keyed by tag name, and variant streams go in variants.
rationale: Each value sits under the spec's name, in the form the spec writes it, so playlist["EXT-X-TARGETDURATION"] reads like the line #EXT-X-TARGETDURATION:6. A uniform { value } wrapper would be more regular but adds a level the spec does not have. -22 says Multivariant, never master.
trigger: Decisions 11 and 12 fixed keys and value types but not how each tag form appears in the output.

decision: EXTINF's duration is number whether written as decimal-floating-point or decimal-integer. It is the one exception to decision 12's one-type-per-spec-type mapping.
rationale: The spec allows either syntax for one quantity in seconds, so decision 12 applied literally would give number | bigint depending on how the server wrote it. An integer duration loses no precision as a number.
trigger: Section 4.4.4.1 defines the duration as 'a decimal-floating-point or decimal-integer'.

decision: Where the spec's format line uses single-letter placeholders, keys use the spec's prose nouns. EXT-X-BYTERANGE:<n>[@<o>] becomes { length, offset }. EXTINF's placeholders match its prose already and become { duration, title }.
rationale: Section 4.4.4.2 describes n as the length of the sub-range and o as a byte offset. Single-letter grammar placeholders are not names, and the style guide's no-abbreviations rule points the same way.
trigger: Applying decision 11 to EXT-X-BYTERANGE, whose format line names its parts n and o.

decision: Carry-forward tags are represented both ways. A segment keeps the tags written before it under their spec names (decision 23). It also gets resolved, library-added fields: keys (a readonly array, since several KEYFORMATs can apply), map, bitrate, byteRange with its offset resolved, mediaSequenceNumber, and discontinuitySequenceNumber. Resolved fields are frozen shared references to the written tag objects, which is a declared exception to the style guide's no-aliases rule. No resolved per-segment program date-time is derived.
rationale: Streamed segment units arrive independently (decision 6), so without resolved fields every streaming caller would have to keep state and reimplement section 4.4.4.4's KEYFORMAT tracking. The written tags are needed for toHLS() to reproduce where each tag appeared. Frozen references are computed once at parse time and cannot drift, which is the rule's concern. Deriving program date-time accumulates floating-point error, so that tradeoff is left to callers.
trigger: Tags such as EXT-X-KEY, EXT-X-MAP, and EXT-X-BITRATE apply to every later segment until the next occurrence.

decision: Date-times (EXT-X-PROGRAM-DATE-TIME, EXT-X-DATERANGE START-DATE and END-DATE) are strings holding the spec text exactly as written, offset and precision included. The schema validates them as ISO 8601 date-times with an offset.
rationale: Only the verbatim string keeps the original offset and precision, which toHLS() needs to reproduce the playlist. It is readonly as a plain value, needs no dependency, and matches decision 12's quoted-string mapping. Date is mutable and loses the offset, and Temporal is native only on Node 26, not Node 22/24 or Safari.
trigger: Decision 26 left program date-time to callers, raising what type date-time values have.

decision: Date-time values are typed as a branded string, DateTime = string & { readonly [dateTimeBrand]: true }, which is a plain string at runtime. Pure exported functions convert them: toDate(value) returns a new Date the caller owns, toEpochMilliseconds(value) returns a number, and toInstant(value, Temporal) takes the Temporal namespace (native or a caller-supplied polyfill). All three come from both entry points. Because their input was validated at parse time, a failed conversion inside them is a library bug, handled by an assertion.
rationale: The brand ensures conversions only receive validated date-times, so they have no failure outcome to return. Taking Temporal as an argument supports polyfilled environments without a dependency. Ready-made revivers would make the whole result unknown (decision 20) and put mutable Dates in readonly output. Methods on tags would need invented names, since EXT-X-DATERANGE has two date fields. A reviver could be built on these functions later.
trigger: The user asked for easy conversion from the decision 27 strings and to discuss options.

decision: Lines the spec says to ignore are kept as raw text in position, as { kind, line } with kind unrecognizedTag, ignoredTag (with a reason citing the section 6.3.1 rule), or comment. They go in a library-added ignored array on the next segment, variant, or the playlist itself for lines at the end. Unrecognized attributes inside an otherwise valid tag go in an ignored array on that tag as raw NAME=value text. Nothing in the typed output depends on ignored content, and unrecognized tags are never parsed generically.
rationale: Section 6.3.1 is met because the playlist's parsed meaning ignores these lines. Keeping raw text lets toHLS() round-trip a playlist and lets callers handle vendor ad tags such as EXT-X-CUE-OUT. Attaching lines to what follows mirrors how the spec attaches segment tags, so streaming units carry their own. A generic parse would guess grammars the spec does not define.
trigger: Section 6.3.1 tells clients to ignore unrecognized tags and attributes, while backlog item 2 asked whether output keeps ignored tags for round-tripping.

decision: Decision 15's context object is renamed options. It holds the substitution context fields (uri, multivariant) and limits: { lineBytesMax, substitutedLineBytesMax, unitCountMax }. Defaults are named constants (initially 1 MiB, 1 MiB, and 1,000,000 units, to be adjusted against benchmarks and real playlists) and can be overridden per call. Exceeding a limit is a separate outcome, { kind: ParseKind.limitExceeded, limit, value }, distinct from malformed, and parse throws a RangeError for it. The overload shapes are unchanged.
rationale: Playlists arrive from the network. Without limits, a source that never sends a newline, or a line of many references to a large variable, exhausts memory, and the style guide requires a limit on everything. Overridable defaults avoid a release for every large but legitimate playlist. A separate outcome lets callers tell an invalid playlist from one larger than they allowed.
trigger: Streaming line buffering, variable substitution expansion, and unit count were unbounded.

decision: Vitest is the test runner, as a development dependency only. It covers runtime tests (test.each for table-driven cases), type-level tests (expectTypeOf for the overloads, the unknown reviver result, the DateTime brand, and per-tag factory types), and benchmarks (bench, for backlog item 3). zod remains the only runtime dependency.
rationale: Much of the design's contract exists only in the types and needs tests that fail at compile time. node:test has no type-level assertions or benchmarking, so it would need about two added packages anyway, and running TypeScript directly depends on Node's type-stripping support across 22.x. One mainstream tool is the smaller supply-chain risk.
trigger: Choosing how to test a library whose contract is largely type-level and which needs a benchmark.

decision: A TypeScript script extracts the 15 embedded playlists from the vendored spec into tests/fixtures/, named by section number, and is rerun whenever the pinned revision changes. Expected outputs are hand-written typed TypeScript constants. Each rule in the decision 8 policy table gets a negative fixture: a valid typed base with exactly one line broken. A test goes through the policy table and asserts that every rule has at least one fixture producing it.
rationale: Generating fixtures from the pinned spec keeps tests as tied to it as the code layout is, and a rerun shows what changed between revisions. The coverage test makes a rule added without a negative test fail CI, so coverage of invalid input is enforced.
trigger: Choosing a source for test fixtures once Vitest was chosen (decision 31).

decision: The module tree mirrors the spec with nested directories, one level per spec level, each named with its full section number and heading (src/4-playlists/4.4-playlist-tags/4.4.6-multivariant-playlist-tags/4.4.6.2-ext-x-stream-inf.ts). Sections with no code get no directory. A section's prose rules live in that section's own file. Library code that belongs to no section (scanner, factory, entry points, date-time functions) lives in src/library/. Each section directory has a barrel that is its public surface.
rationale: Each part of the path is a table-of-contents heading, and the full number in every name makes a file unambiguous on its own. Plain alphabetical sorting puts 10 before 2, but no level of -22 that holds code exceeds 9.
trigger: Decision 1 committed to mirroring the spec's layout without saying how.

decision: This library is a full rebuild of github.com/harrietfigueroa/streaming-hls-parser and is published as streaming-hls-parser. The default entry is streaming-hls-parser and the precompiled entry is streaming-hls-parser/precompiled. Each exports an HLS namespace object (parse, safeParse) plus named type and date-time function exports, with identical types. license, author, repository, and bugs carry forward from the existing package.json. engines, the separate browser bundle, the optional debug peer dependency, ts-node, and the install and npm devDependencies are replaced as consequences of decisions 22 and 31 and the style guide's no-logging-in-pure-code rule.
rationale: The rebuild keeps the existing package name and its npm history (0.1.0 through 0.1.4).
trigger: Claude proposed the name fast-hls-parser for the package.

decision: No code from the existing streaming-hls-parser repository is read. Only its package.json and its test data are read. It has no fixtures directory, so the test data is the four playlists in examples/*.m3u8. Listing the repository's file paths, without opening the files, was used to find them.
rationale: The rebuild is designed from the spec and the decisions in this log, not from the previous implementation.
trigger: The user identified the library as a rebuild of streaming-hls-parser.

decision: The rebuild ships as streaming-hls-parser 0.2.0.
rationale: Published versions are 0.1.0 through 0.1.4, and ^0.1.4 does not accept 0.2.0, so existing users stay on the old code until they upgrade on purpose. 1.0.0 would lock in the toString/toHLS/toJSON design (backlog item 2) before it exists. 1.0.0 can follow once the API has been exercised against the real-world corpus (backlog item 5).
trigger: npm is at 0.1.4 while the repository's package.json says 0.1.0, so the rebuild's version must sort after 0.1.4.

decision: toHLS() returns the playlist's HLS text, round-tripping exactly (ignored lines and written tag positions included), and toString() returns the same text. Any normalized form would be an option on toHLS() (for example toHLS({ canonical: true })), never a different toString().
rationale: This follows the builtin convention (URL.prototype.toString returns href), so string conversion of a playlist always produces a playlist. Two names producing different text would leave callers guessing which is which.
trigger: Backlog item 2 open question 1: how toString() and toHLS() differ.

decision: Output objects implement toJSON(), which converts each bigint to its decimal string and leaves every other value unchanged. Its return type is Jsonified<T>, a mapped type replacing bigint with string throughout. The JSON form is for output and is not meant to be read back: HLS.parse(playlist.toHLS()) is the round trip.
rationale: Without toJSON(), JSON.stringify throws on decision 12's bigints, breaking logging, caching, and HTTP responses. Decimal strings are lossless where number is not. A number-or-string conversion would give integer fields a type that depends on the value. Replacers still work, because JSON.stringify calls toJSON() first.
trigger: Backlog item 2 open question 2. The user replied by asking for toStream() as well, which Claude read as approving option 2. The user has not confirmed that reading.

decision: The user explicitly confirmed decision 38: toJSON() converts each bigint to its decimal string and leaves everything else unchanged.
rationale: Decision 38 rested on Claude's reading of the user's reply, and this records the explicit confirmation.
trigger: The user confirmed the toJSON choice directly.

decision: toStream() returns a ReadableStream<Uint8Array> of UTF-8 bytes, one chunk per unit (a segment, a variant, or a block of playlist-level tags). It is built on a pull-based source, so chunks are produced only when the consumer reads and memory stays bounded to one unit. Internally it pulls from the same generator that toHLS() uses. It belongs to playlist objects from a static parse.
rationale: The name promises a stream, and ReadableStream is native on every target, so new Response(playlist.toStream()) works without conversion. Bytes are what Response, fetch bodies, and Node writables accept, mirroring decision 21's byte input. Sharing the generator with toHLS() keeps the two from drifting apart.
trigger: The user added toStream() to the output object methods.

decision: Streamed units implement toHLS(), toString(), and toJSON(). unit.toHLS() returns the unit's lines exactly as written (its ignored lines, its preceding tags, and its URI), so joining every unit's text in order reproduces the input. A test asserts that each unit's text matches what that unit contributes to the static playlist's toHLS().
rationale: Filtering or rewriting a playlist as a stream, such as dropping ad segments, needs per-unit serialization and never holds the whole playlist. toStream() already serializes one unit per chunk (decision 40), so this exposes code that exists anyway.
trigger: Decision 40 placed toStream() on static playlists only, leaving open whether streamed units serialize.

decision: Playlists and units carry their methods on a shared, frozen prototype for each object kind. The final step of each unit's schema copies the parsed value into an Object.create(prototype) object and freezes it. Tag objects stay plain data with no methods. Object.setPrototypeOf is not used on zod output.
rationale: This is how builtins such as URL and Date carry methods. Object.keys, spreads, and for...in see only spec data, and the cost per object is one prototype link. Freezing the prototype stops callers from replacing methods globally. Per-object defineProperty costs about four definitions per unit, and enumerable methods would pollute the data.
trigger: Backlog item 2 open question 3: how methods attach to readonly output objects.

decision: Each parsed unit keeps its raw source lines in a private, non-enumerable slot, and its toHLS() returns them exactly, with variable references and formatting preserved. HLS.stringify(value), the counterpart to JSON.stringify, writes any playlist or unit value from its data alone in the canonical form, so it works on spreads and hand-built values. toHLS({ canonical: true }) is HLS.stringify(this). No retainSource option is added until backlog item 7 shows retained-text memory matters.
rationale: Parsed data loses formatting (EXTINF:6.00000 becomes 6), attribute order, and pre-substitution references, so decision 37's exact round trip needs the raw lines. Frozen objects mean callers build new values, and a spread drops decision 42's prototype methods, so prototype-free serialization is needed. HLS.stringify completes the parse/stringify parallel with JSON. Retained text is proportional to input, which decision 30 bounds.
trigger: Backlog item 2 open question 4 (pre-substitution text) showed that exactness requires raw lines and that data a caller modified had no serialization path.

decision: HLS.stringify(value, replacer?) takes a replacer that follows JSON.stringify exactly: replacer.call(holder, key, value) on each property before it is written, children after parents, undefined omits the property, and an array acts as an allowlist of keys. There is no space parameter. A later formatting option would go in an options object in a later position.
rationale: This is decision 20's JSON parity applied to the mirror-image function, so replacers written for JSON.stringify keep working. HLS is line-based with no indentation, so space has nothing to control. Omitting it makes a passed space a type error, where accepting and ignoring it would be a silent no-op.
trigger: Decision 43 introduced HLS.stringify, raising its signature relative to JSON.stringify.

decision: This directory becomes a checkout of harrietfigueroa/streaming-hls-parser on a rebuild branch created from origin/main. The first commit removes the old tree with git rm, without reading the files (decision 35). Then work/ and spec/ are committed, and the implementation follows. Shipping is a pull request into main that the user merges. The old .github publishing workflow and trusted-publishing setup are config and may be read to decide whether to keep them.
rationale: Only a branch with shared history can ship through a reviewable pull request without force-replacing main, which the user's git rules forbid. The old code stays reachable in history without anyone reading it.
trigger: The working directory was not a git repository, and the rebuild belongs to the existing streaming-hls-parser repository.

decision: The CDN browser bundle is kept. esbuild (a development dependency) produces two self-contained ESM files with zod included, dist/browser/index.js and dist/browser/precompiled.js, matching decision 17's two entries. The publish workflow keeps uploading them as release assets and posting CDN links. The package exports map is unchanged, so bundler users never load the bundled zod. The workflow's trusted publishing (OIDC, --provenance, on release published) is kept.
rationale: Earlier releases documented direct CDN imports of a self-contained browser file. The unbundled ESM build imports zod as a bare specifier, which a browser without a bundler cannot resolve. Relying on a third-party rewriting service such as jsDelivr /+esm is unverified for the two entries.
trigger: Reading the old .github/workflows/publish.yml (allowed as config by decision 45) showed release steps uploading dist/index.browser.js and posting CDN links, which decision 34 had dropped.

decision: The zod benchmark lives in bench/ and is kept in the repository. It starts with prototype tag schemas in the shape decision 16 describes and is updated to use the library's real schemas once the full types exist. It measures per-tag safeParse from raw tag to typed value (EXTINF, EXT-X-STREAM-INF, EXT-X-PART, EXT-X-PROGRAM-DATE-TIME), with and without z.compile, where a compile with strict: true proves each compiled case actually compiled. It also measures a hand-written conversion of the same tags as a floor, and the 11,701-segment fixture through a minimal line loop.
rationale: A benchmark has no behavior to drive test-first, so its plan was presented before writing. Keeping it means the measurement can be rerun against the real schemas instead of being rebuilt.
trigger: Starting backlog item 3. The user approved the plan and asked to keep the benchmark and update it once the full types are made.

decision: The benchmark supports decisions 16-18, and they stand unchanged. Compiled zod schemas run within about 8% of hand-written conversion per tag (EXTINF 10.44M vs 10.61M ops/s, EXT-X-PROGRAM-DATE-TIME 21.26M vs 23.09M, EXT-X-STREAM-INF 2.03M vs 2.01M, EXT-X-PART 12.00M vs 11.60M) and 5% on the 11,701-segment fixture (2.51 ms vs 2.39 ms mean). The uncompiled runtime parser, which is the default entry, is 1.4-3x slower per tag but 31% slower on the fixture (3.13 ms). Claude's estimate of tens of milliseconds for a 10,000-segment playlist was about 10x too high.
rationale: These are measured on one machine (Apple Silicon, Node 24.21.0, zod 4.6.7, Vitest 5.1.0) with prototype schemas, two tags per segment in the fixture loop, and no attribute scanning, so they bound zod's share of the cost rather than the parser's total. The first run was invalid because Vitest's module runner read imports through export getters on every call for the runtime and hand-written cases only. Reading each export once into a local removed every warning, and these are the corrected numbers.
trigger: Backlog item 3, the benchmark that decisions 16-18 depended on.

decision: Tag validation and conversion stay in zod, not hand-written code.
rationale: Compiled zod matches hand-written speed (decision 48), so zod's advantages carry it. Each rule is written once: the four prototype tags took 34 lines of schema against 116 hand-written. Output types derive from the schemas instead of being kept in sync by hand. Failures carry structured paths and reasons for malformed issues. The costs are a runtime dependency, a 30% slower uncompiled default, and the unavailability of z.coerce, recursive schemas, and async transforms.
trigger: The user asked whether zod has any advantage over hand-written conversion, after the benchmark showed compiled zod matching it.

decision: Every MUST or MUST NOT in section 4 that constrains the playlist file defaults to malformed, per section 4's opening clause (spec line 633). Section 4 MUSTs directed at clients are behavior rules, not playlist rules. Rules outside section 4, chiefly section 6's server responsibilities, default to violation. This also amends decision 10: section 4.4.3.1's rule that rounded EXTINF durations not exceed the Target Duration defaults to malformed. The decision 8 policy table is unchanged in shape, and only these defaults move.
rationale: Section 4 opens by stating that its MUST and MUST NOT rules define legal playlists and that clients MUST fail to parse playlists violating them. Decision 8 chose the spec's own line, and this clause is that line. The earlier inventory missed it by searching only for the phrase 'fail to parse'. Section 4 holds about 147 MUST sentences, of which roughly 20 direct clients (a text-pattern count). A spec-conformant default rejects playlists players accept, which a lenient policy addresses (backlog item 10).
trigger: Reading section 4 before building section 4.1 turned up the opening clause.
